title: The nine duties of the dental nurse
blurb: The nine duties the discussion is built on, a way to remember them, and how they link to your Diploma units and the GDC Standards.
question: Ten minutes into your Professional Discussion, the assessor says: "Tell me about a time you raised a concern at work." Which of the nine duties are you being asked to show, and how do you keep your answer within your role?

teach.body: NEBDN says the Professional Discussion is based on "the nine duties of the Dental Nurse". NEBDN's public specification doesn't print the list, but the national occupational standard for dental nurses (Dental nurse, GDC 2023, reference ST1431) sets out exactly nine duties, and the Diploma's ten units line up with them. Think of them as the whole dental nurse role split into nine areas. Your provider can confirm how they present them.

teach.word: All Teeth Can Look Pearly If Our Routine Works

letters.sub: Duty 2: support treatment planning and onward referral
Duty 3: communicate, keep confidentiality and records
Duty 4: lead and work in partnership
Duty 5: judgement, integrity, scope, law and ethics
Duty 8: review and develop your own practice
Duty 9: your own and the team's

teach.h: The duties and the units they match
head: Duty
In short
Unit
teach.caption: Matched by unit title. Unit 10 (Respond to Risks and Medical Emergencies) feeds into the clinical duties, 1 and 2.
Blue: clinical. Teal: people and teamwork. Purple: professional and ethical. Green: health and growth.

teach.body: The standard lists eight behaviours that apply to all nine duties. They include compassion, integrity and honesty, taking personal responsibility for your actions, managing your time, being open and honest when things go wrong (the professional duty of candour), respecting whether patients want to take part in training, upholding the GDC Standards for the Dental Team, and a willingness to learn. However the duty is phrased, these behaviours are what you show in every example.

teach.text: Don't confuse the nine DUTIES with the GDC's nine PRINCIPLES. Both lists have nine items. The duties describe what a dental nurse does. The principles (Standards for the Dental Team) are the ethical standards every registrant must meet. In the discussion you use the principles to explain WHY you carried out a duty the way you did.

teach.h: One example can show several duties
teach.body: Raising a concern is a good illustration. It is part of acting as a professional (duty 5), it needs clear communication and an accurate record (duty 3), it may mean leading by speaking up within the team (duty 4), and it is backed by GDC principle 8, "Raise concerns if patients are at risk". The GDC is clear that your duty to raise concerns overrides any personal or professional loyalties.

teach.h: Raising a concern: the usual route

steps.label: Notice a risk to patients
steps.sub: Own or others' health, behaviour or performance

steps.label: Raise it early
steps.sub: With the person, if safe, or your line manager

steps.label: Escalate if not resolved
steps.sub: e.g. NHS body, CQC (England) or the GDC

steps.label: Record what you did
steps.sub: Dates, who you told, what was said

teach.caption: People who raise concerns honestly should be protected from discrimination or other detriment. The external body depends on the UK nation and the type of concern.

items: Nine duties: Assessment, Treatment & referral, Communication, Leadership, Professional practice, Inclusion, Oral health, Reflection, Well-being.
Mnemonic: All Teeth Can Look Pearly If Our Routine Works.
They come from the national dental nurse standard and line up with the Diploma's units.
Eight behaviours, including candour and upholding GDC Standards, apply to every duty.
Duties = what you do; GDC principles = the standards that explain why.

summary: You can now list the nine duties of the dental nurse in order, remember them with a mnemonic, match them to your Diploma units, tell them apart from the GDC's nine principles, and see how one workplace example such as raising a concern can evidence several duties at once.

A.q: Which of these is NOT one of the nine duties of the dental nurse?
options: Promote oral health to individuals and the wider population
Reflect on, review and develop the quality of own practice
Diagnose oral disease and plan the patient's treatment
Manage own health and well-being and that of the team
A.why: Dental nurses support assessment and treatment planning, but the GDC Scope of Practice is clear that dental nurses do not diagnose disease or plan treatment.

A.q: In the mnemonic "All Teeth Can Look Pearly If Our Routine Works", what does the "I" stand for?
A.why: I is duty 6: practise in a non-discriminatory and inclusive manner, recognising culture, equality and diversity.

whyNot.0: Infection control sits within the clinical duties (1 and 2), not its own duty.
whyNot.2: Instrument care is a clinical task within duty 2.
whyNot.3: Indemnity is part of professional practice (duty 5), not a duty in its own right.

A.q: A learner says, "The nine duties are the same as the GDC's nine principles." What is the best correction?
options: Correct: the GDC wrote both lists for dental nurses
Correct: the principles were renamed duties in 2023
Wrong: the duties apply only to dentists
Wrong: duties describe the role; principles set standards
A.why: The duties describe what a dental nurse does; the GDC Standards' nine principles are the ethical standards all registrants must meet, which you use to justify your actions.

whyNot.0: They are two different lists with different purposes.
whyNot.1: The GDC principles were not renamed; they remain the Standards for the Dental Team.
whyNot.2: The nine duties are specifically the dental nurse's duties.

B.q: Which duty does "Communicate effectively, maintaining confidentiality and records appropriately" describe?
B.why: Duty 3 covers communication, confidentiality and record keeping.

whyNot.1: Duty 1 covers clinical tasks relevant to assessment and diagnosis.
whyNot.2: Duty 5 covers autonomous professional practice within scope.
whyNot.3: Duty 8 covers reflecting on and developing your own practice.

B.q: Which behaviour, applying to every duty, means being open and honest with patients when something goes wrong?
B.why: The professional duty of candour means being open and honest with patients, carers, colleagues and employers when things go wrong.

whyNot.0: Consent is the patient's permission for treatment, not openness about errors.
whyNot.1: Advocacy means speaking up for a patient's needs, not admitting a mistake.
whyNot.3: Delegation is passing a task to a competent colleague.

B.q: You notice a colleague repeatedly skipping instrument cleaning to save time. Which GDC principle most directly backs you raising it?
options: Principle 8: raise concerns if patients are at risk
Principle 5: have a clear complaints procedure
B.why: Skipping decontamination puts patients at risk, and GDC principle 8 requires you to raise concerns when that happens.

whyNot.0: Principle 2 is about communicating with patients, not reporting unsafe practice.
whyNot.2: Principle 3 is about consent to treatment.
whyNot.3: Principle 5 is about handling patient complaints.

C.q: Which Diploma unit lines up most closely with duty 8, "Reflect on, review and develop the quality of own practice"?
options: Unit 3: Communication in the Dental Setting
C.why: Reflecting on and developing your practice is the heart of CPD, Unit 9.

whyNot.0: Unit 7 matches duty 7, promoting oral health.

C.q: Where are the nine duties of the dental nurse set out as a numbered list?
options: In the national occupational standard for dental nurses
In the GDC Standards for the Dental Team booklet
In the public NEBDN Diploma qualification specification
C.why: The Dental nurse (GDC 2023) occupational standard lists nine duties, and the Diploma's units line up with them. NEBDN's public specification names the duties but doesn't list them.

whyNot.1: The GDC Standards contain nine principles, not the nine duties.
whyNot.2: NEBDN's public specification refers to the nine duties without listing them.
whyNot.3: HTM 01-05 is decontamination guidance, not a list of duties.

C.q: When raising a concern about a colleague's practice, what is usually the best first step if it is safe to do so?
options: Post about it on a private social media group
Raise it with the person or your line manager
Wait until you have collected proof
C.why: Raising it early and locally, with the person or your manager, is usually the first step. You escalate if it isn't resolved or isn't safe to raise locally.

whyNot.0: Discussing colleagues on social media breaches professional standards.
whyNot.1: The police are only relevant to criminal matters, not the usual first step.
whyNot.3: The GDC does not require proof before you raise a concern.

reteach.title: A day in the surgery, duty by duty
reteach.question: Can you spot all nine duties in one ordinary working day?

blocks.body: You check the next patient's medical history and record the dentist's charting (duty 1). You set up, assist and arrange the follow-up the dentist prescribes (duty 2). You calm an anxious patient and write accurate notes (duty 3). You show a new trainee how to load the washer-disinfector (duty 4). You decline a task you aren't trained for (duty 5). You book an interpreter (duty 6). You give brushing advice (duty 7). You jot down a reflection (duty 8). You take your break and check in on a stressed colleague (duty 9).

blocks.text: Duties 1 and 2 say tasks "relevant to" assessment, diagnosis and treatment planning. That means supporting them. It never means making the diagnosis or the plan yourself.

explain.body: Routine clinical and technical tasks that support assessment and diagnosis (duty 1) and treatment planning and onward referral (duty 2). The dentist diagnoses and plans; you record, prepare, assist and monitor.

test.q: Recording the dentist's charting during an examination evidences which duty?
test.why: Charting supports the assessment and diagnosis of patients, which is duty 1.

explain.body: Duty 3 is communication, confidentiality and records. Duty 4 is professional leadership, working in partnership with patients, the dental team and other health and social care professionals.

test.q: You show a new trainee how to process instruments safely and check their work. Which duty is this mainly evidence for?
test.why: Training and supporting a colleague is professional leadership within the team, duty 4.

whyNot.0: Processing instruments is clinical, but the focus here is leading a colleague.
whyNot.1: Duty 8 is reflecting on your own practice.

explain.body: Duty 5 is acting as an accountable professional within scope and the law. Duty 6 is practising in a non-discriminatory and inclusive way, recognising culture, equality and diversity.

test.q: Arranging a professional interpreter for a patient who speaks little English best evidences which duty?
test.why: Removing a language barrier so the patient gets equal care is inclusive practice, duty 6 (and it supports duty 3, communication).

whyNot.3: Duty 8 is reflection on your own practice.

explain.body: Duty 7 is promoting oral health to individuals and communities. Duty 8 is reflecting on and developing your own practice. Duty 9 is managing your own health and well-being and supporting the team's.

test.q: After a difficult appointment you write down what happened, what you learned and what you'll do differently. Which duty is this?
test.why: Reflecting on and developing the quality of your own practice is duty 8.

whyNot.0: Duty 3 covers patient records, but a personal reflection is about developing your practice.
